subject: Chemistry
scope: Eight original single-fact AQA AS Chemistry RP5 and RP6 exam-theory recall cards based on reported data and interpretation only; no experimental procedures.
notes: Extends existing original 69-mark RP4–RP6 exam-question scenarios from v202. Avoids repeating basic test colours, test procedures, apparatus set-up and arithmetic already covered. No claim of full-spec or past-paper completion.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why may a measured boiling point differ from a reference value even for the same pure liquid?
cards.back: Boiling temperature depends on external pressure.
accept: Boiling temperature depends on external pressure.
A change in atmospheric pressure changes the boiling point.
Because boiling point varies with pressure.
Different pressures can give different boiling temperatures.
reject: The liquid must be a different substance.
Boiling point is independent of pressure.
All pure liquids boil at exactly 100 °C.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does percentage recovery measure in a distillation data question?
cards.back: The percentage of the target material initially present that is recovered.
accept: The percentage of the target material initially present that is recovered.
Recovered target mass divided by initial target mass, times 100.
The fraction of available target substance recovered, expressed as a percentage.
The recovered amount of target divided by the starting amount of target, multiplied by 100.
reject: Recovered mass divided by the theoretical mass of product from a reaction.
The percentage of liquid that is a new chemical product.
The percentage purity of the recovered liquid.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does a narrow boiling range alone not prove the identity of a distilled liquid?
cards.back: Different liquids may have similar boiling temperatures; other evidence is needed.
accept: Different liquids may have similar boiling temperatures; other evidence is needed.
A narrow boiling range suggests purity but cannot uniquely identify a liquid.
Several compounds can have similar boiling points, so a second identification method is needed.
Boiling data alone cannot establish the exact molecular identity.
reject: A narrow range proves the molecular formula.
Any liquid with a narrow range is completely pure and identified.
Boiling temperature is unrelated to molecular identity.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is simple distillation less effective for separating liquids with very similar boiling points?
cards.back: Both liquids can contribute substantially to the vapour.
accept: Both liquids can contribute substantially to the vapour.
The vapour contains appreciable amounts of both similar-boiling components.
Their volatilities are similar, so neither component is strongly enriched by one vaporisation.
The components vaporise over overlapping temperature ranges.
reject: The liquids must have identical chemical formulas.
A condenser chemically converts both liquids into one substance.
The more volatile liquid can never evaporate.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can an oxidation-test colour change alone fail to distinguish a primary from a secondary alcohol?
cards.back: Both primary and secondary alcohols can be oxidised.
accept: Both primary and secondary alcohols can be oxidised.
Both types can give a positive oxidation result.
Primary and secondary alcohols both react in an oxidation test.
Oxidation is possible for both primary and secondary alcohols.
reject: Only tertiary alcohols can be oxidised.
Primary alcohols cannot be oxidised.
A positive oxidation test always proves the alcohol is primary.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does a negative aldehyde-specific test not, by itself, prove that an unrestricted unknown is a ketone?
cards.back: Other functional groups can also give a negative result.
accept: Other functional groups can also give a negative result.
Many non-aldehydes besides ketones also test negative.
A negative aldehyde test does not rule out every other functional group.
A negative result alone does not uniquely identify a ketone.
reject: Every negative result proves the unknown is a ketone.
All non-aldehydes must be ketones.
A negative aldehyde test proves the sample is an aldehyde.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What can a positive functional-group test suggest without proving the entire molecular structure?
cards.back: The presence of a functional group, not a unique complete structure.
accept: The presence of a functional group, not a unique complete structure.
A likely functional group but not the whole molecule.
The test supports a functional-group assignment rather than one exact structure.
A reaction pattern consistent with a group but not full identity.
reject: The exact carbon skeleton and every atom position.
The only possible structural isomer.
The complete molecular formula and unique structure in every case.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is agreement between different recorded observations more useful than one organic test result?
cards.back: Independent evidence reduces ambiguity between possible structures.
accept: Independent evidence reduces ambiguity between possible structures.
Several matching observations narrow the set of possible identities.
Combining different tests helps rule out alternative structures.
Independent results strengthen the functional-group assignment.
reject: One observation always proves the entire structure.
Multiple identical observations automatically eliminate every impurity.
Additional evidence is never needed to identify a molecule.
